module_title: Understanding Agricultural Produce and Quality Standards

lessons.title: Major Categories of Agricultural Produce: Grains, Legumes, Tubers, Fruits, Vegetables
lessons.body: As a produce sourcer, you must know the five main categories of agricultural produce because each has different handling, quality checks, and market demands. Grains include maize, rice, millet, sorghum, and wheat. They are dry, storable, and traded in large volumes. In Africa, maize is the most traded grain. A 50 kg bag of maize might sell for $15-$25 depending on region and season. Legumes include beans, cowpeas, groundnuts, and soybeans. They are rich in protein and often traded in smaller quantities. A 50 kg bag of beans can fetch $40-$80. Tubers are root crops like cassava, yam, sweet potato, and Irish potato. They are bulky, perishable, and heavy. A tonne of cassava might sell for $100-$200. Fruits include mangoes, oranges, bananas, pineapples, and avocados. They are highly perishable and need quick handling. A crate of mangoes (about 20 kg) might sell for $10-$20. Vegetables include tomatoes, onions, peppers, and leafy greens. They are delicate and have short shelf life. A basket of tomatoes (about 50 kg) can sell for $20-$50. When sourcing, you must match your category to your logistics: grains and legumes need dry storage, tubers need cool, dark places, and fruits and vegetables need cold chain or quick turnover. Knowing these differences helps you plan transport, storage, and quality checks. For example, you cannot mix onions with leafy greens because onions emit gases that spoil greens. Always ask farmers about variety and season because that affects price and quality. Your profit depends on buying the right category at the right time.

lessons.title: Quality Parameters: Moisture Content, Purity, Size, Color, and Grade
lessons.body: Quality is the difference between profit and loss in produce sourcing. The five key parameters are moisture content, purity, size, color, and grade. Moisture content is the percentage of water in the produce. For grains, safe storage moisture is 12-14% for maize, 12-13% for rice, and 9-10% for groundnuts. If moisture is too high, mold grows and aflatoxins develop, which are poisonous. You can test moisture with a simple moisture meter (costs $50-$200) or by biting a grain: if it shatters, it's dry; if it's chewy, it's wet. Purity means freedom from foreign matter like stones, dirt, chaff, and other seeds. A 50 kg bag of clean beans should have less than 1% foreign matter. You can check by taking a handful and sorting. Size matters for grading: large, uniform produce fetches higher prices. For example, large onions (above 5 cm diameter) sell better than small ones. Color indicates maturity and freshness. Bright green vegetables are fresher than yellowing ones. Uniform color means uniform ripening. Grade is a combination of these parameters. In many African markets, grades are A, B, C: Grade A is premium, Grade B is fair, Grade C is poor. For export, grades are stricter. You must learn to assess each parameter quickly. Use your senses: sight, touch, smell. A moisture meter, a weighing scale, and a grading sieve are basic tools. Always document your quality checks. If you buy poor quality, you lose money. If you buy high quality, you can negotiate better prices. Train your eye and hand to judge quality in seconds.

lessons.title: Local and International Quality Standards (e.g., FAO, ISO, GlobalG.A.P.)
lessons.body: Quality standards are rules that define what is acceptable produce. Local standards are set by national bureaus of standards, like KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria, or SABS in South Africa. These often mirror international standards but are adapted to local conditions. FAO (Food and Agriculture Organization) provides guidelines for moisture, defects, and contaminants. For example, FAO sets maximum aflatoxin levels in groundnuts at 10 ppb (parts per billion) for human consumption. ISO (International Organization for Standardization) has standards like ISO 22000 for food safety management. GlobalG.A.P. is a private standard for good agricultural practices, focusing on food safety, worker welfare, and environmental sustainability. To export to Europe, your produce often must be GlobalG.A.P. certified. Certification costs money and requires record-keeping, but it opens premium markets. For local markets, you may only need to meet basic national standards. As a sourcer, you must know which standard your buyer requires. If you buy from farmers who don't follow standards, your produce may be rejected. You can help farmers understand standards by sharing simple checklists: no mold, no stones, correct moisture. Many African countries have export promotion agencies that provide free guides. Always ask for a certificate of analysis when buying large volumes. For small-scale sourcing, you can use a refractometer to check sugar content in fruits (Brix level) or a moisture meter for grains. Standards are not just paperwork; they protect your reputation and your customer's health. Start by meeting local standards, then aim for international ones as you grow.

lessons.title: Post-Harvest Handling and Its Impact on Quality
lessons.body: Post-harvest handling is everything that happens after harvest until the produce reaches the buyer. Poor handling causes up to 50% losses in Africa. The key steps are harvesting, cleaning, sorting, drying, storage, and transport. Harvest at the right maturity. For maize, harvest when husks are dry and kernels are hard. For tomatoes, harvest at breaker stage (pinkish) for transport, not fully red. Cleaning removes dirt and stones. Use a simple sieve or winnowing. Sorting removes damaged and diseased produce. Drying is critical for grains: dry on a clean tarpaulin, not on the ground, to avoid contamination. Sun-drying to 12-14% moisture takes 2-3 days. For tubers, curing (drying the skin) for 2-3 days helps them store longer. Storage must be dry, cool, and pest-free. Use hermetic bags (like GrainPro) for grains to prevent weevils without chemicals. For fruits and vegetables, cold storage (0-10Â°C depending on type) extends shelf life. Transport quickly and carefully. Avoid throwing bags; use crates for fruits. A bruise on a mango can cause rot within a day. If you handle well, you reduce losses and get higher prices. For example, well-dried maize can sell for 20% more than poorly dried maize. Train your farmers on these steps. Provide them with tarpaulins, crates, and hermetic bags if possible. Your profit depends on how well you manage post-harvest. Always inspect produce before buying; if it's wet, dirty, or bruised, either reject it or pay less. Good handling is a competitive advantage.

lessons.title: Common Defects, Adulteration, and How to Detect Them
lessons.body: Defects and adulteration are common in African produce markets. Defects include mold, insect damage, discoloration, and physical damage. Adulteration is when someone adds cheaper materials to increase weight or volume. For example, groundnut powder may be mixed with cassava flour, or chili powder with brick dust. To detect defects, use your senses. Look for mold: green or black spots on grains, or a musty smell. Insect damage: holes in grains or webbing. Discoloration: off-color produce. For adulteration, do simple tests. For groundnuts, take a handful and smell: if it smells like cassava, it's adulterated. For grains, put a sample in water: stones sink, chaff floats, and pure grain settles in between. For honey, adulterated with sugar syrup, put a drop on your thumb: pure honey spreads slowly; adulterated spreads fast. For milk, use a lactometer. For spices, rub between fingers: pure spices leave color and aroma; adulterated leave little. Aflatoxin is a serious defect in groundnuts and maize. You can use a simple aflatoxin test kit (costs $5-$10 per test) or send samples to a lab. If you suspect aflatoxin, reject the produce. Always buy from trusted farmers and visit their fields. Build relationships so you know their practices. When buying, inspect at least 10% of bags. Open bags and check bottom and top. Adulteration often happens at the bottom. If you find adulteration, blacklist that supplier. Your reputation depends on selling clean produce. Teach your farmers about the dangers of adulteration; it ruins markets for everyone. Stay vigilant.

lessons.title: Hands-On Practice: Grading and Sorting Produce Samples
lessons.body: This lesson is practical: you will grade and sort produce samples. You need samples of maize, beans, tomatoes, and onions. You also need a moisture meter, a weighing scale, a sieve, and a clean table. Start with maize. Take 1 kg. Check moisture with a meter. If above 14%, dry it more. Then sort: remove broken kernels, stones, and moldy grains. Weigh the good maize. Calculate percentage of good maize. For Grade A, you need 98% good, less than 1% broken, and no mold. For beans, check for insect damage and discoloration. Grade A beans are uniform in size and color, with less than 2% defects. For tomatoes, sort by size and ripeness. Grade A tomatoes are firm, uniform red, and 5-7 cm diameter. Remove bruised and green ones. For onions, grade by size: large (above 5 cm), medium (3-5 cm), small (below 3 cm). Remove soft or sprouted onions. Record your results in a notebook: sample weight, defect weight, grade. Practice until you can grade a 50 kg bag in 15 minutes. This skill is what buyers pay for. You can also train farmers to pre-grade, so you buy already sorted produce at a lower price. Always use clean containers. After grading, pack in clean bags or crates. Label the grade. Take photos of your graded produce to show buyers. This hands-on practice builds your confidence and your business. Repeat with other produce like rice, groundnuts, and peppers. The more you practice, the faster and more accurate you become. Your ability to grade consistently will set you apart from other sourcers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Grading, Sorting & Quality Control for African Produce Sourcing

This practical reference is your field manual for buying, inspecting, and accepting agricultural produce in African markets. Whether you are sourcing maize in Tanzania, cassava in Nigeria, beans in Uganda, or mangoes for export from Ghana, your margin depends on buying the right quality at the right price â and rejecting what will lose you money downstream. This lesson covers hands-on grading and sorting, defect detection, adulteration checks, and the standards frameworks (FAO, ISO, GlobalG.A.P.) that govern local and international trade.

Why Quality Control Is a Profit Centre, Not a Cost

In African produce sourcing, quality failures are expensive: a rejected export container, aflatoxin-contaminated groundnuts, or moisture-laden maize that molds in storage. Buyers who grade properly at the point of purchase pay less for lower grades, avoid post-purchase losses, and build a reputation that commands premium contracts. Grading is therefore a commercial discipline, not a bureaucratic one.

1. Major Categories of Agricultural Produce in African Sourcing

Each category has distinct handling and quality profiles:

  • Grains: Maize, rice, sorghum, millet, wheat. High volume, moisture-sensitive, aflatoxin risk in maize.
  • Legumes: Beans, cowpea, groundnut, soybean. Bruchid (weevil) damage, aflatoxin in groundnut.
  • Tubers: Cassava, yam, sweet potato, Irish potato. Bruising, rot, short shelf life.
  • Fruits: Mango, banana, pineapple, avocado. Ripeness stage, cold chain, export grade.
  • Vegetables: Tomato, onion, pepper, leafy greens. Perishability, wilting, microbial load.

2. Quality Parameters You Must Measure

Buy on measurable parameters, not on appearance alone. The five core parameters are moisture content, purity (foreign matter), size/uniformity, color, and grade. Moisture is the single most important commercial parameter for grains and legumes because it drives mold, aflatoxin, and weight loss.

Table 1: Typical Quality Parameters by Produce Category (African trade context)
Produce Moisture (max) Purity / Foreign Matter Defect Tolerance Key Risk

Rice (paddy)14%â¤ 1%â¤ 5% chalkyMold, breakage
Beans (common)13%â¤ 1%â¤ 3% weevilBruchid damage
Groundnut9%â¤ 1%â¤ 2% shrivelledAflatoxin (high)
Cassava (chips)14%â¤ 2%â¤ 5% moldyCyanide, rot
Mango (export)â0% soilâ¤ 5% blemishFruit fly, anthracnose

Source: Compiled from FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius standards and East African Community (EAC) maize and legume standards (EAS 2:2017, EAS 46:2017).

3. Local and International Quality Standards

Know which standard your buyer requires before you buy. Local standards (e.g., KEBS in Kenya, NAFDAC/SON in Nigeria, TBS in Tanzania) govern domestic trade. International standards open export markets:

  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius: Baseline food safety and commodity standards; aflatoxin limits (e.g., 10â15 ppb for groundnut).
  • ISO 22000 / ISO 9001: Food safety management and quality management systems.
  • GlobalG.A.P.: Good Agricultural Practice certification required by many EU and UK retailers.
  • Organic (EU/USDA): For premium organic export contracts.
Table 2: Aflatoxin and Moisture Reference Limits for Key African Export Crops
Crop Moisture for safe storage Aflatoxin limit (Codex/EU) Primary market
Groundnut (human)â¤ 9%4â15 ppb totalEU, regional
Maize (human)â¤ 13.5%10â20 ppb totalRegional, WFP
Maize (animal feed)â¤ 14%20â50 ppb totalLocal feed mills
Dried cassava chipsâ¤ 14%10 ppb totalRegional, EU
Sesameâ¤ 8%4 ppb total (EU)EU, Asia

Source: FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius (CODEX STAN 193-1995, revised) and EU Regulation 2023/915 on contaminants in food.

4. Post-Harvest Handling and Its Impact on Quality

Post-harvest losses in Sub-Saharan Africa are estimated at 30â40% for perishables and 10â20% for grains (FAO/APHLIS). The quality you buy is a function of how the farmer dried, threshed, and stored the crop. Practical controls:

  • Drying: Sun-dry on tarpaulins, not bare ground, to reduce soil contamination and moisture.
  • Threshing: Avoid mechanical damage that creates entry points for mold.
  • Storage: Hermetic bags (PICS, GrainPro) control insects without chemicals and reduce aflatoxin risk.
  • Cold chain: For fruits and vegetables, pre-cooling and refrigerated transport preserve grade.
  • Traceability: Lot tagging enables recall and protects your brand if a buyer rejects a consignment.

5. Common Defects, Adulteration, and How to Detect Them

Adulteration is common in African produce trade and directly erodes your margin. Detect it with simple field tests:

  • Sand/stones in grains: Weigh a sample, sieve, weigh residue; compare to contract purity limit.
  • Water added to increase weight: Use a moisture meter; if absent, squeeze test and salt-and-bottle test for grains.
  • Mixing old and new stock: Check color, smell, and insect frass; old stock is duller and may smell musty.
  • Dye in spices/chilli: Rub on wet white cloth; artificial color bleeds.
  • Aflatoxin: Visual mold, discolored kernels, and a bitter smell are warning signs; confirm with a rapid test kit (e.g., lateral flow).
  • Foreign matter in groundnut/sesame: Sieve and hand-sort a 1 kg sample; record percentage.
â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â AFLATOXIN:

Aflatoxin is a carcinogen and can be fatal in high doses. Never taste or chew suspect groundnut, maize, or cassava to test quality. Wear gloves and a dust mask when handling moldy lots. Do not blend contaminated grain with clean grain to "dilute" aflatoxin â this is illegal in most markets and endangers consumers. Reject and quarantine suspect lots, and report to your buyer and local standards authority (e.g., KEBS, NAFDAC, TBS).

6. Hands-On Practice: Grading and Sorting Produce Samples

Run this exercise with a 1 kg sample of maize, beans, or groundnut:

  1. Weigh the sample and record total weight.
  2. Sieve to separate foreign matter (sand, stones, chaff); weigh and calculate % impurity.
  3. Hand-sort into: sound, broken/discolored, moldy, insect-damaged; weigh each fraction.
  4. Measure moisture with a meter (or salt-bottle test if unavailable).
  5. Assign grade using your buyer's specification (e.g., Grade A â¤ 1% foreign matter, â¤ 2% broken, moisture â¤ 13.5%).
  6. Calculate value using current market price per grade and decide buy/renegotiate/reject.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Confirm buyer's grade specification and standard (local vs. export) before purchase.
  • â Measure moisture with a calibrated meter; reject above contract limit.
  • â Sieve and weigh a 1 kg sample for foreign matter and calculate %.
  • â Hand-sort for mold, discoloration, and insect damage; record defect %.
  • â Check for adulteration (sand, water, dye, old stock) using field tests.
  • â Verify traceability: farm origin, harvest date, storage method.
  • â Quarantine suspect lots; never blend contaminated with clean produce.
  • â Document lot, grade, weight, price, and test results for every purchase.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • FAO â Food and Agriculture Organization (FAOSTAT and commodity standards)
  • FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius â international food standards
  • APHLIS â African Postharvest Losses Information System
  • GlobalG.A.P. â Good Agricultural Practice certification
  • ISO 22000 â Food Safety Management Systems

Business takeaway: Grade at the point of purchase, buy on measurable parameters, and document every lot. In African produce sourcing, disciplined quality control is the difference between a profitable contract and a write-off.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a grain?
quiz.explanation: Maize is a cereal grain, while cassava is a tuber, tomato is a vegetable, and groundnut is a legume.

quiz.q: What is the safe storage moisture content for maize?
quiz.explanation: Maize should be stored at 12-14% moisture to prevent mold and aflatoxin growth.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to measure moisture content in grains?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter directly measures the percentage of water in grains.

quiz.q: What does purity mean in produce quality?
quiz.explanation: Purity refers to the absence of stones, dirt, chaff, and other foreign materials.

quiz.q: Which grade is considered premium?
quiz.explanation: Grade A is the highest quality grade, with strict parameters for defects, size, and color.

quiz.q: What does GlobalG.A.P. stand for?
quiz.explanation: GlobalG.A.P. is a private standard for Good Agricultural Practices focusing on food safety and sustainability.

quiz.q: Which organization sets maximum aflatoxin levels in groundnuts?
quiz.explanation: FAO provides guidelines for contaminants, including aflatoxin limits in groundnuts.

quiz.q: What is the first step in post-harvest handling?
quiz.explanation: Harvesting at the right maturity is the first step, followed by cleaning, sorting, etc.

quiz.q: Why should grains be dried on a tarpaulin rather than on the ground?
options: B) To avoid contamination with dirt and stones
quiz.explanation: Drying on the ground can introduce dirt, stones, and moisture from the soil, reducing quality.

quiz.q: What is curing in tuber post-harvest handling?
options: B) Drying the skin for 2-3 days
quiz.explanation: Curing involves drying the skin of tubers to extend storage life.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common adulterant in groundnut powder?
quiz.explanation: Cassava flour is a cheap filler often mixed with groundnut powder to increase weight.

quiz.q: How can you detect adulteration in honey?
options: A) Put a drop on thumb and see if it spreads fast
quiz.explanation: Pure honey spreads slowly on the thumb, while adulterated honey with sugar syrup spreads quickly.

quiz.q: What is a sign of aflatoxin contamination in maize?
quiz.explanation: Green or black mold on maize is a common indicator of aflatoxin-producing fungi.

quiz.q: When grading tomatoes, what is the ideal diameter for Grade A?
quiz.explanation: Grade A tomatoes are typically firm, uniform red, and 5-7 cm in diameter.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of sorting produce?
options: B) To remove damaged and diseased items
quiz.explanation: Sorting removes defective produce, ensuring only good quality items are sold.

quiz.q: Which of these is a tuber?
quiz.explanation: Yam is a tuber, while rice is a grain, cowpea is a legume, and mango is a fruit.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for groundnuts?
quiz.explanation: Groundnuts should be stored at 9-10% moisture to prevent mold and aflatoxin.

quiz.q: Which standard is often required for exporting to Europe?
quiz.explanation: GlobalG.A.P. certification is commonly required for exporting fresh produce to Europe.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of post-harvest losses in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Poor post-harvest handling, including inadequate drying, storage, and transport, causes up to 50% losses.

quiz.q: Which of these is a physical defect in grains?
quiz.explanation: Broken kernels are a physical defect, while high moisture and aflatoxin are chemical/microbial issues.

quiz.q: How can you test for stones in grains?
quiz.explanation: Stones sink in water, while chaff floats, and pure grain settles in between.

quiz.q: What is the role of a refractometer in quality checks?
quiz.explanation: A refractometer measures Brix, which indicates sugar content in fruits and juices.

quiz.q: Which of these is a legume?
quiz.explanation: Soybean is a legume, while millet is a grain, sweet potato is a tuber, and cabbage is a vegetable.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to check when buying a bag of maize?
quiz.explanation: Moisture content is critical because high moisture leads to mold and aflatoxin.

quiz.q: Which practice helps prevent insect damage in stored grains?
quiz.explanation: Hermetic bags create an airtight environment that kills insects without chemicals.

quiz.q: What is adulteration?
options: A) Adding cheaper materials to increase weight
quiz.explanation: Adulteration is the addition of inferior substances to increase weight or volume for higher profit.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of good quality onions?
quiz.explanation: Good quality onions are firm, dry, and uniform in size, without sprouts.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a grading sieve?
options: B) To separate produce by size
quiz.explanation: A grading sieve is used to separate produce based on size, such as grains or seeds.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect bags when buying a large lot?
quiz.explanation: Inspecting at least 10% of bags helps detect adulteration and defects without checking every bag.

quiz.q: What is the recommended action if you detect aflatoxin in groundnuts?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is dangerous to health, so the produce must be rejected to protect consumers.
